intro: In the 1800s, prizefighting was a crime in most states. Yet newspapers filled pages with it, and later radio carried fights live into millions of homes. At the same time, reformers in Chicago and New York built gyms in settlement houses, parks and Ys so that city children had somewhere to play.

This unit visits two kinds of city rooms. One is the fight night, sold by promoters and papers and watched over by state commissions. The other is the neighborhood court: the Hull House gym, the park field house, the Black Y, the Harlem ballroom and the playground hoop.

You will read laws, books and records from these rooms. You will be able to explain who built each room, who paid for it, who was let in or kept out, and how newspapers and radio made city sport a public story.
bigQuestion: Who built the city's rooms for boxing and basketball, and who decided who could use them?

test.q: What was the last heavyweight title fight fought with bare knuckles?
test.why: The 1889 Sullivan–Kilrain fight in Mississippi was the last bare-knuckle heavyweight title fight.

test.q: Who ran the National Police Gazette and used it to promote boxing?
test.why: Richard K. Fox took over the Gazette in 1877 and gave out prizes and belts.

test.q: Which law created New York's state athletic commission?
test.why: The 1920 Walker Law legalized boxing under a state commission.

test.q: What did the Sims Act ban?
choices: Carrying prizefight films across state lines
test.why: The 1912 Sims Act banned interstate transport of fight films.

test.q: Where did Joe Louis win the heavyweight title in 1937?
choices: The Olympic Club in New Orleans
test.why: Louis beat James Braddock at Comiskey Park on June 22, 1937.

test.q: Who founded Chicago's Catholic Youth Organization in 1930?
test.why: Bishop Bernard Sheil founded the CYO, which ran a large boxing program.

test.q: Why did the NCAA end college boxing championships after 1960?
choices: A college boxer died after a bout in the 1960 tournament
test.why: Charlie Mohr of Wisconsin died after the 1960 tournament, and the NCAA dropped boxing.

choices: The first settlement house, in London
test.why: Toynbee Hall opened in East London in 1884 and inspired Hull House.

test.q: In which 1909 book did Jane Addams argue for public places to play?
choices: The Spirit of Youth and the City Streets
test.why: Addams made the case in The Spirit of Youth and the City Streets.

test.q: What did Chicago's 1905 field houses hold?
test.why: Field houses held gyms, baths, a library branch and meeting rooms.

test.q: Which group, founded in 1906, pushed cities to build playgrounds?
choices: The New York State Athletic Commission
test.why: The Playground Association of America formed in 1906 with Gulick as first president.

test.q: Why was the Wabash Avenue YMCA built?
choices: Many Y branches would not admit Black Chicagoans
test.why: Segregation kept Black people out of many Ys, so a South Side branch opened in 1913.

test.q: Where did the New York Renaissance play home games?
choices: A park field house in Chicago
test.why: The Rens played at the Renaissance Casino ballroom in Harlem.

test.q: How did boxing and basketball differ in Illinois schools?
choices: The IHSA ran boxing but never basketball
Both were run by the IHSA from 1900
The IHSA ran basketball but never boxing
Neither was ever played in Illinois
test.why: Basketball had an IHSA state series; boxing stayed in town gyms and tournaments.

test.q: What did newspapers and radio do for both sports in the city?
choices: They built every gym and park
They wrote the rule books for both
They turned games and fights into public stories followed by people far away
test.why: Papers ran tournaments and stories, and radio carried events live to distant listeners.

write.prompt: Who had the most power over city sport in this unit: newspapers, reformers or government? Argue your answer using at least three named records from the unit, such as the Sims Act (1912), the Walker Law (1920), Addams's 1909 book or the 1905 field houses.
tips: Name each law, book or event with its year.
Say who built or paid for each room you describe.
Include who was let in and who was kept out.
Compare two kinds of power before you choose one.
Use unit words such as athletic commission, settlement house and recreation.
